description: We are a motivated team with a strong academic and practical background in robotics, artificial intelligence, and interdisciplinary STEM applications. Our collective interests focus on leveraging technology and scientific knowledge to develop innovative solutions to global and space-related challenges, in line with the mission of the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary:
We developed Inmonia, an offline-capable health companion for astronauts on long-duration missions. It turns a short daily check-in about mood, sleep, and physical symptoms into a practical plan for the day. An astronaut who misses home might get a five-minute voice-note guide, while someone who reports too little privacy might get a suggestion to set aside quiet time. When a symptom affects movement, the prototype can hold a scheduled exercise session and help the astronaut prepare a summary for crew medical.

On missions far from Earth, astronauts may need to decide what to do before ground support responds. Inmonia gives crew members a way to take a manageable next step, record whether it helped, and spot recurring symptoms over time. The check-in and guides work offline after the first load.
details:
How it works. The check-in opens at login and asks one question at a time. Crew members can skip individual questions, resume saved progress, and use a rotatable 3D body map to record where discomfort occurs and whether it affects movement. Inmonia follows up on previously logged symptoms. A rule-based engine then suggests up to three actions, explains why each fits, and links to a short guide. An evening reflection records what helped, and 7- and 30-day views make recurring symptoms easier to spot.

What makes it creative. The same low mood rating can lead to different plans. The demo lets judges switch between homesickness and low privacy to see how context changes the recommendation. A third scenario shows how the prototype holds an exercise session when a symptom warrants review. The astronaut chooses which details to export and can share them through their mission’s designated medical channel. Mission patches reward checking in and following up regardless of reported mood or pain.

How we used NASA resources. The Advanced page uses NASA’s career effective spaceflight radiation dose standard as a reference for the corresponding reading. It also displays published measurements from Curiosity’s Radiation Assessment Detector to illustrate the radiation environment during the cruise to Mars and at Gale Crater. NASA photographs illustrate all 17 guides.

What we built it with. We used React, TypeScript, and Vite for the web app, and Three.js with a MakeHuman mesh for the interactive body map. Browser storage saves progress, and a service worker caches the app and guides for offline use. We tested desktop and mobile flows with Playwright and deployed the prototype on Render. The demo runs in a browser with no custom hardware.

Design considerations and intended impact. We designed for limited connectivity, low interaction effort, and crew control over sensitive information. The intended impact is to help astronauts act on everyday concerns sooner and bring a clearer symptom history to crew medical when they need support.
